report:
# Conclusion

**The claim that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans is not supported by current evidence.** Capsaicin has only been shown to have anti-proliferative, apoptosis-inducing, and cell-cycle-arresting effects on breast cancer cells (e.g., MDA-MB-231, MCF-7, BT-20) in laboratory (in vitro) studies, working through mechanisms such as modulation of the EGFR/HER-2 pathway and induction of G2/M cell cycle arrest (nature.com/articles/onc2009335; spandidos-publications.com). These are preclinical, cell-culture findings, not evidence that capsaicin cures or treats cancer in living patients.

No human clinical trials have tested capsaicin as an actual cancer treatment for breast cancer. The only breast-cancer-related human trials found (CAPTRANE, QUCIP) evaluated topical high-concentration capsaicin patches for managing chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy and post-surgical nerve pain in breast cancer patients — a pain-management application, not an anti-tumor treatment (mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11763653/).

Reviews explicitly note that capsaicin's clinical anticancer efficacy remains "currently limited," constrained by poor bioavailability and side effects (burning sensation, gastrointestinal pain) that hinder its use as an oral anticancer agent (frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full). A broader review of capsaicin and cancer likewise concludes the compound's clinical value to complement chemotherapy remains "speculative" (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). Epidemiological data on chili pepper intake and cancer risk are also mixed and inconsistent, offering no support for a therapeutic claim.

**Bottom line:** Capsaicin shows anticancer activity against breast cancer cells in lab settings, but there is no clinical trial evidence it treats breast cancer in humans; its proven human application is limited to pain relief, not tumor treatment.
